definition.text: The ability to consume and save that a person, household or firm gains over a set period, usually counted in money.

facts.text: Income is hard to define and its meaning differs between fields; economic income can differ from income as defined by law.
US tax law counts wages, salary, profit, interest, rent and other earnings received in a calendar year as household income.
For a firm, gross income can be defined as all revenue minus the cost of goods sold.
Borrowing or repaying money is not income under any definition, but interest and forgiven debt are.
Non-monetary joys, such as watching a sunset, are not counted as income, so reported income may misstate well-being.
Education raises income by increasing workers' skills and productivity.
Income is conventionally written as Y in economics.

definition.text: A widely used economic definition of income as consumption plus the change in a person's net worth.

facts.text: The definition dates from 1938 and counts both what is consumed and the change in the value of property held.
Taxable income is usually lower than Haig–Simons income, since unrealized gains such as a rise in share prices are economic but not taxable income.
'Full income' adds non-monetary consumption ability to money income, but it cannot be observed, forcing reliance on money income.

definition.text: The income earned from the factors of production: rent from land, wages from labor, interest from capital and profit from enterprise.

facts.text: In consumer theory, income is the budget a person can spend on different goods at their given prices.
National income is divided among the factors of production through the factor market.

definition.text: The extent to which income is spread unevenly across a population.

facts.text: It can be measured with tools such as the Lorenz curve and the Gini coefficient.
Many economists argue some inequality is necessary but excessive inequality causes efficiency problems and social injustice.
UN Sustainable Development Goal 10 aims to reduce inequality.
Globalization tends to raise a country's average income, but unequally.

title: Measures of national income and output
article: Measures of national income and output

definition.text: The family of statistics, such as GDP, GNI and net national income, used to estimate the total economic activity of a country or region.

facts.text: All of them count the total goods and services produced within an economy and its sectors.
Adjusted national income is net national income corrected for the depletion of natural resources.
Systematic national accounts began only in the 1930s in the United States and some European countries, spurred by the Great Depression and Keynesian economics.
Goods and services are counted at market value, the price they fetch, not their actual usefulness.
Three methods give market values for all output: the product, expenditure and income methods.
Some measures count only goods and services exchanged for money, while others impute values for bartered goods.

title: Avoiding double counting
article: Measures of national income and output#Output

definition.text: The rule that national output counts only the final value of a good, or the value added at each stage, not every sale along the chain.

facts.text: If meat is worth $10 at the farm, $30 at the butcher and $60 at the supermarket, $60 enters national output, not the $100 sum.
The values added at each stage, $10, $20 and $30, sum to the same final value.
GDP at market price equals the value of output minus intermediate consumption.

title: Gross, net, domestic and national
article: Measures of national income and output#Expenditure

definition.text: The naming scheme of national income measures, combining gross or net, national or domestic, and product, income or expenditure.

facts.text: 'Gross' means total product, while 'net' subtracts the amount needed to offset depreciation of fixed capital.
'Domestic' counts everything produced inside a country's borders; 'national' counts everything produced by its nationals anywhere.
A French-owned cotton factory in Senegal counts in Senegal's domestic figures but France's national figures.
Net domestic product is GDP minus depreciation of capital.

title: National income as a welfare measure
article: Measures of national income and output#National income and welfare

definition.text: The question of how well GDP per person reflects people's welfare, given what it leaves out.

facts.text: Countries with higher GDP may also score higher on other welfare measures such as life expectancy.
A paid nanny's income counts in GDP, but a parent's unpaid childcare does not.
Cleaning up an oil spill adds to GDP, while the lost well-being from fouled beaches is not measured.
Alternatives include the Human Development Index, Index of Sustainable Economic Welfare, Genuine Progress Indicator and sustainable national income.
